title: G7 to Release 100 Million Barrels of Oil and Diesel to Ease Prices
summary:
The G7, a group of advanced economies, has agreed to release 100 million barrels of oil and diesel to ease supply pressures that have caused fuel prices to rise sharply. A barrel is a standard unit for measuring oil.

The G7 includes the United States, the United Kingdom, Canada, Japan, Germany, Italy and France, with the European Union also represented at its meetings. In a joint statement, the group said the move would include a "substantial release" of diesel in the coming days.

President Donald Trump had threatened to ban diesel exports from the U.S. That would have eased pressure on prices for U.S. consumers ahead of November's midterm elections, but it would have pushed up prices elsewhere. The G7 said member countries agreed to "refrain from export restrictions on energy and energy products" on one another.

Diesel is used heavily by the haulage industry and in agriculture, so higher fuel costs feed into essentials such as food. After a meeting chaired by French President Emmanuel Macron, the G7 agreed to release reserves of "up to 100 million barrels" within four months, coordinated by the International Energy Agency, or IEA. The plan includes a frontloaded substantial diesel release within the first 20 days by G7 members and partners.

Macron said the coordinated action would "bring down the prices of petroleum products, particularly diesel." He also noted the agreement not to pursue export bans, saying Trump "was very clear on this point." Speaking at the White House, Trump later said an export ban on diesel was "never really on the table."

It is not yet clear which partner countries will release stocks, or how quickly. The 100 million barrels will be a mix of diesel and crude oil. The price of global benchmark Brent crude briefly dropped below $100 a barrel but rose back to around $102 by Friday evening. Before the U.S. and Israel invaded Iran, it was trading at around $73. Matt Smith, director of commodities research at Kpler, said oil rose again due to renewed strikes between Saudi Arabia and the Houthis in Yemen. G7 leaders also said they will coordinate maintenance schedules so multiple refineries are not shut down at the same time, and encourage countries to refine more diesel.
why_it_matters: Diesel moves food and goods, so changes in its price can feed into the cost of everyday essentials for families and businesses.

questions.question: Why did President Trump threaten to ban diesel exports?
options: To punish farmers who sell diesel abroad before the election
To stop oil from being sold to the G7 member countries
To help European refineries open earlier than they had planned
To ease prices for U.S. consumers, though prices would rise elsewhere
questions.correct_answer: To ease prices for U.S. consumers, though prices would rise elsewhere

questions.question: What mix will the 100 million barrels include?
options: Gasoline and natural gas
Diesel and crude oil
Only diesel from the U.S.
Only crude oil from Japan

questions.question: How quickly will the diesel part start, according to the plan?
options: No release until the November midterm elections end
A large release in the first 20 days
A small test release at a single refinery
A large release only after four months pass
questions.correct_answer: A large release in the first 20 days

questions.question: What is still unclear about the release?
options: Whether the G7 will ever hold another meeting
Whether Macron was invited to chair the meeting
Which partner countries will release stocks and how quickly
Whether trucks and farms will ever use diesel
questions.correct_answer: Which partner countries will release stocks and how quickly

questions.question: What happened to Brent crude by Friday evening?
options: It stayed above $102 all day long
It briefly dropped below $100, then rose to about $102
It fell to about $73 and stayed there
It dropped below $100 and stayed there
questions.correct_answer: It briefly dropped below $100, then rose to about $102
